question: In the Norwegian registry-based longitudinal study, what were the peak median HbA1c levels for females and males during late adolescence, and at what ages?
passage_1: The study Glycemic control and complications in patients with type 1 diabetes – a registry-based longitudinal study of adolescents and young adults evaluates longitudinal glycemic control, the prevalence of microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy), and the impact of transition timing from pediatric to adult care among 874 young people with type 1 diabetes in Norway using data linked from two nationwide registries. The study found that median HbA1c peaked in late adolescence at 9.3% for females at age 17 and 9.1% for males at age 19, with overall target HbA1c levels achieved by very few participants (only 11% of adolescents aged 14–17 and 7% of young adults aged 18–25). Microvascular complications were prevalent, with 16% of participants exhibiting retinopathy and 13% exhibiting nephropathy; higher HbA1c levels across adolescence and young adulthood, longer diabetes duration, younger age at diagnosis, and smoking were strongly associated with a higher risk of complications. Additionally, patients who transferred to adult care before age 18 had significantly higher HbA1c levels and a higher prevalence of complications than those who transferred between ages 18–22, while less than 40% of patients with albuminuria were receiving recommended ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment. Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.
passage_2: The study Hemoglobin A1c Levels and Risk of Severe Hypoglycemia in Children and Young Adults with Type 1 Diabetes from Germany and Austria: A Trend Analysis in a Cohort of 37,539 Patients between 1995 and 2012 evaluates temporal trends in the association between hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and the risk of severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemic coma in a prospective cohort of 37,539 children and young adults with type 1 diabetes from Germany and Austria between 1995 and 2012. The study found that the relative risk for severe hypoglycemia and coma per 1% HbA1c decrease declined significantly from 1.28 to 1.05 and from 1.39 to 1.01, respectively, over the 18-year period, alongside a continuous increase in daily blood glucose monitoring frequency, short- and long-acting insulin analog use, and continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion pump therapy. Based on these findings, the paper indicates that lower HbA1c levels have become a minor predictor for severe hypoglycemia, allowing clinicians and young patients with type 1 diabetes to aim for near-normal glycemic control to prevent long-term diabetic complications without substantially increasing their risk of severe hypoglycemic events.
passage_3: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

question: What does the paper on HbA1c measurement for diagnosis of type 2 diabetes in children recommend as the preferred screening method for at-risk pediatric populations?
passage_1: Screening and Diagnosis of Prediabetes and Diabetes in US Children and Adolescents evaluates the performance of American Diabetes Association risk-based screening criteria and current clinical definitions of prediabetes and diabetes—based on HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), or both—to identify high cardiometabolic risk in US youth aged 10 to 19 years. The study found that while 25.5% of US youth met screening criteria, the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria were low for detecting hyperglycemia. Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.
passage_2: Hemoglobin A1c measurement for the diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes in children evaluates the utility, reliability, and methodology of using laboratory-based HbA1c testing for diagnosing Type 2 diabetes in pediatric populations, addressing recent studies that dismissed HbA1c due to poor correlation with Oral Glucose Tolerance Tests (OGTT) or Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG). The authors find that rejecting HbA1c based on lack of correlation with OGTT or FPG is scientifically flawed because neither OGTT nor FPG have themselves been validated against long-term health outcomes (such as retinopathy) in children, and OGTT suffers from low reproducibility. Additionally, non-fasting HbA1c screening is more practical, reproducible, and has been shown to increase diabetes screening rates and early detection among adolescents. The paper recommends that American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic criteria remain useful for screening at-risk, asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic pediatric populations, with laboratory-based HbA1c certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) being the preferred method; practitioners should exercise clinical judgment when diagnostic test results conflict, and HbA1c should be avoided in cases of pregnancy, cystic fibrosis, or hemoglobinopathies and disorders causing high red blood cell turnover.

It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.

question: According to the clinical report on promoting optimal development, what are the recommended ages for child-focused mental health, emotional, and behavioral screening?
passage_1: The clinical report Promoting Optimal Development: Screening for Mental Health, Emotional, and Behavioral Problems evaluates the increasing prevalence of mental health, emotional, and behavioral (MEB) issues among children and outlines updated guidance for pediatric primary care clinicians to effectively screen, identify, and manage these conditions. The report notes that 13% to 20% of U.S. children have a diagnosed MEB disorder—with ADHD, anxiety, disruptive behavior, and mood disorders being the most common—and highlights rising suicide rates alongside exacerbated post-pandemic mental health distress. To address significant gaps in detection and a severe shortage of subspecialist clinicians, the guidelines recommend starting caregiver-focused screening within the first month of life for postpartum depression, followed by child-focused MEB screening at 6, 12, 24, and 36 months, alternating with developmental and autism screenings, and continuing annually after age 3. Additionally, the clinical report provides recommendations on using standardized, culturally responsive screening tools, managing positive screens within the pediatric medical home, promoting family resilience, and overcoming practice-level barriers to streamline workflow and improve care integration.

passage_1: The article Psychological interventions for adherence, metabolic control, and coping with stress in adolescents with type 1 diabetes: a systematic review evaluates the variations in effectiveness among psychological interventions—specifically cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), coping skills training (CST), stress management, and psychotherapy—on adherence, metabolic control, and coping with stress in adolescents with type 1 diabetes based on a review of 24 studies published between 1990 and 2019. The findings indicate that while behavioral interventions utilizing CBT principles have a superior positive impact on regimen adherence, metabolic control improves significantly through CST and certain CBT approaches, and stress management and psychotherapy show strong promise in helping adolescents manage daily diabetes-related stressors. Consequently, the review suggests that psychological interventions hold promise for enhancing diabetes management in youth, though additional research is required to better understand their specific effects.
passage_2: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.

The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. question: In the SENCE study, what were the effects of CGM combined with a family behavioral intervention versus CGM alone versus standard blood glucose monitoring on time spent in hypoglycemia?
passage_1: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.
passage_2: The Strategies to Enhance New CGM Use in Early Childhood (SENCE) study evaluates the effects of continuous glucose monitoring combined with a family behavioral intervention (CGM+FBI) and CGM alone compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) over six months in children aged 2 to <8 years with type 1 diabetes. The findings demonstrate that while consistent CGM use over six months did not produce significant improvements in percent time in range (70–180 mg/dL), it significantly reduced mean time spent in hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL) across both CGM groups compared to BGM, with the family behavioral intervention additionally providing clear benefits for parental well-being by reducing diabetes burden and fear of hypoglycemia.
passage_3: The study Youth Involvement in the Decision to Start CGM Predicts Subsequent CGM Use evaluates whether youth involvement in the decision to initiate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) influences subsequent CGM adherence, and tests whether CGM self-efficacy and perceived hassle mediate this relationship among parent-youth dyads. The findings reveal that youth involvement in the initial decision positively predicted CGM use between weeks 5 and 12, mediated by the youth perceiving higher self-efficacy and lower hassle at a 2-month follow-up. Based on these findings, the authors recommend that healthcare providers actively facilitate youth participation and input when deciding to initiate CGM therapy in order to maximize long-term device adherence and clinical benefits.

passage_1: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.
passage_2: Family-based Psychoeducation and Care Ambassador Intervention to Improve Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Trial evaluates the impact of a 2-year randomized clinical trial testing three levels of care—standard care with basic care coordination, monthly outreach by a Care Ambassador (CA), and monthly CA outreach plus quarterly family-based psychoeducation—on glycemic control (A1C), parental involvement, family conflict, and quality of life among 153 youth with type 1 diabetes. The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. Based on these findings, the authors implicitly recommend incorporating structured psychoeducational strategies—focused on teamwork, setting realistic expectations, and joint problem-solving—alongside routine care coordination specifically for youth with suboptimal glycemic control, while cautioning against relying solely on frequent phone or email outreach without targeted behavioral support

question: According to the hemoglobin a1c measurement for diagnosis of type 2 diabetes in children research, evaluates HbA1c for T2D diagnosis in children?
passage_1: Hemoglobin A1c measurement for the diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes in children evaluates the utility, reliability, and methodology of using laboratory-based HbA1c testing for diagnosing Type 2 diabetes in pediatric populations, addressing recent studies that dismissed HbA1c due to poor correlation with Oral Glucose Tolerance Tests (OGTT) or Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG). The authors find that rejecting HbA1c based on lack of correlation with OGTT or FPG is scientifically flawed because neither OGTT nor FPG have themselves been validated against long-term health outcomes (such as retinopathy) in children, and OGTT suffers from low reproducibility. Additionally, non-fasting HbA1c screening is more practical, reproducible, and has been shown to increase diabetes screening rates and early detection among adolescents. The paper recommends that American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic criteria remain useful for screening at-risk, asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic pediatric populations, with laboratory-based HbA1c certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) being the preferred method; practitioners should exercise clinical judgment when diagnostic test results conflict, and HbA1c should be avoided in cases of pregnancy, cystic fibrosis, or hemoglobinopathies and disorders causing high red blood cell turnover.
passage_2: Screening and Diagnosis of Prediabetes and Diabetes in US Children and Adolescents evaluates the performance of American Diabetes Association risk-based screening criteria and current clinical definitions of prediabetes and diabetes—based on HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), or both—to identify high cardiometabolic risk in US youth aged 10 to 19 years. The study found that while 25.5% of US youth met screening criteria, the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria were low for detecting hyperglycemia. Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.

Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

question: What IFG: 16.0%, hrA1C: 3.2% (IFG 5x more common) according to the diabetes screening with hemoglobin a1c versus fasting plasmglucose in multiethni study?

In this multiethnic 6th-grade cohort of 3,980 students, IFG was five times more common than hrA1C (16.0% vs. 3.2%), but hrA1C was more persistent over a two-year period into 8th grade (59.4% vs. 46.9%). High-risk A1C was strongly associated with non-Hispanic Black race/ethnicity, family history of diabetes, higher BMI, waist circumference, and fasting insulin, whereas IFG was associated with Hispanic ethnicity, male sex, higher BMI, waist circumference, fasting insulin, high blood pressure, and mean triglycerides. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.
